https://www.live95fm.ie/news/live95-news.text: Search Limerick's Live 95 On Air Now Shannon Airport nominated for top global aviation award All Live95 News Thursday, 20 August 2026 12:52 By Tara Byrne Share on Facebook Share on X Share on Whatsapp Via Shannon Airport Group The winners will be announced in Germany in October. Shannon Airport has been named a finalist in the 'Under 5 Million Passengers' category at the upcoming Routes World Awards 2026. The awards recognise airports for route development, airline partnerships, and marketing efforts aimed at increasing passenger traffic. The shortlisting comes during a period of growth for the airport, with Shannon currently offering 40 destinations, its highest total in 17 years. This includes five new European routes added this year: Madrid, Rome, Frankfurt, Warsaw, and Poznan. Ray O’Driscoll, CEO of The Shannon Airport Group, said the nomination reflects the team's effort to expand regional transport links. "We are delighted to be shortlisted for the Routes World Awards 2026," O’Driscoll said. "This recognition reflects the strength of the partnerships we have built with our airline customers and the commitment of our aviation development team to growing connectivity for the Mid-West and wider region." "This nomination acknowledges the strategic work we have undertaken to attract new services, support route growth, and create opportunities that benefit tourism, business, and regional economic development," he added. Judges evaluate entries based on route development strategy, commercial performance, marketing support for airlines, and traffic growth initiatives. The winners will be announced at the Routes World event in Frankfurt on October 22. Photograph: John Harrington Productions Hudson river plane crash ‘Miracle on the Hudson’ pilot Chesly Sullenberger inducted into US Aviation Hall of Fame Sullenberger landed a disabled passenger plane safely in the Hudson River in 2009 without any loss of life Marina Dunbar Sat 26 Sep 2026 15.54 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 15.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Capt Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger III – the pilot known for safely landing a US Airways flight in New York City’s Hudson River during a 2009 emergency – has been inducted into the US’s National Aviation Hall of Fame, two months after he went public with an Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis. Sullenberger, 75, received the honor during a ceremony held in Washington DC on Thursday, 17 years after he engineered what has become widely known as the Miracle on the Hudson. His actions that day – which saved more than 150 lives – set the stage for him to be inducted alongside the six-member 2026 hall of fame class, including Nasa astronauts and aviation researchers. Pilot known for ‘Miracle on the Hudson’ river plane landing reveals Alzheimer’s diagnosis Read more Sullenberger participated in the ceremony remotely by video, saying: “I want to congratulate the other [inductees] on lifetimes of accomplishments. And I thank you for the honor of enshrinement in the National Aviation Hall of Fame.” During his remarks, he recognized that the dramatic events of 2009 – which were eventually the basis of a Tom Hanks movie – played a major role in his enshrinement. But he made it a point to say: “My career was much more than one flight. “From a very young age, I knew I wanted to fly airplanes. That was the beginning of a lifetime following that dream. I was so fortunate to spend an entire working lifetime doing something I loved.” A former member of the US air force, Sullenberger was piloting US Airways Flight 1549 on 15 January 2009. The aircraft had departed New York City’s LaGuardia airport en route to Charlotte, North Carolina, carrying 150 passengers and five crew members. Not long after takeoff, the aircraft struck a flock of birds, resulting in a total loss of thrust from both engines. Sullenberger ultimately realized that the plane would not be able to make it back to LaGuardia – so he instead landed the aircraft in the Hudson River. All 155 people aboard survived. Sullenberger in July disclosed that he had been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, which had given him another way to think about public service. “This new phase of my life has challenged what it means to be of service,” he said in a statement shared at the time. “And the answer is to speak up. It is my hope that by sharing this, other families living in the shadows with this disease will feel they too can step forward.” Speaking in an interview on Wednesday with the ABC program Good Morning America , Sullenberger described his reaction to learning of the diagnosis. He said he experienced “all those emotions, the shock, the anger, why me?” “We’re part of this community who are trying to make the best of a bad situation.” Figures from the Alzheimer’s Association indicate that about 7.4 million people who are age 65 or older are living with clinical Alzheimer’s dementia. Roughly three out of four are 75 or older. “This is a disease – not a character flaw,” his wife, Lorrie Sullenberger, said on Good Morning America. “I think we need to talk about it more openly, and maybe other people can do the same.” Explore more on these topics Hudson river plane crash Air transport Washington DC news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
